findings.paper_title: 8. Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 Audit Committee 27 July 2026 v2
findings.headline: Investment interest income fell £1.54m short of budget (£966k actual vs £2.12m budgeted)
findings.detail: The council earned only £966,039 in interest on its investments, against a budgeted £2.12m. The paper attributes this directly to reduced investment balances caused by service budget overspends and SEND provision deficits.
findings.matters: This shortfall is a direct consequence of reserve drawdown to cover service deficits, and it reduces the income available to offset borrowing costs and treasury management expenses.
findings.figures: £966k actual vs £2.12m budget; shortfall of £1.54m
findings.quote: interest earned over the course of the year of £966k was £1.54m lower than the budget of £2.12m

findings.paper_title: 8. Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 Audit Committee 27 July 2026 v2
findings.headline: Treasury management costs exceeded budget by £654k (6.4% overspend)
findings.detail: The overall revenue cost of treasury activity (interest payments, minimum revenue provision, debt management) was £10.831m against a budget of £10.177m. The overspend suggests treasury headroom is tighter than planned.
findings.matters: Treasury costs are largely fixed and crowding-out for service spending. A budget miss here indicates broader cash pressures are forcing higher-than-expected borrowing or refinancing costs.
findings.figures: £654k overspend (£10.831m actual vs £10.177m budget)
findings.quote: the overall cost of £10.831m exceeded the revenue budget of £10.177m by £654k

findings.paper_title: 8. Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 Audit Committee 27 July 2026 v2
findings.headline: Council is using short-term borrowing (25 bps cheaper than PWLB) betting on rate cuts by December 2027 for refinancing
findings.detail: Rather than borrowing from PWLB in 2025/26, the council used short-term loans from other local authorities at rates averaging 25 basis points below PWLB rates. The strategy explicitly depends on interest rates falling by around December 2027 to refinance into longer-term PWLB borrowing at better terms. Market expectations are cited as the basis for this assumption.
findings.matters: If rates do not fall as forecast, or fall too slowly, the council faces refinancing risk at higher rates than currently assumed, adding to treasury costs. This is an active rate-bet rather than passive debt management.
findings.figures: Short-term money market rates during year averaged 25 basis points lower than PWLB rates; base rate fell from 4.50% to 3.75%
findings.quote: Current local authority lending rates are significantly lower than equivalent PWLB rates, enabling the Council to achieve substantial savings on interest costs. Short-term money market rates during the year were on average 25 basis points lower than PWLB rates.

findings.paper_title: 8. Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 Audit Committee 27 July 2026 v2
findings.headline: Internal borrowing of £7.025m used for capital will require replacement with PWLB borrowing in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council funded £7.025m of its £63.237m capital programme using internal borrowing (drawing down cash balances) rather than external borrowing. The paper states explicitly: 'There will be a need to replace the internal borrowing with long-term PWLB borrowing during the next financial year.' This creates a known refinancing requirement.
findings.matters: This refinancing need will add to the council's external debt and borrowing costs in 2026/27. It also signals that current liquidity is tight enough that the council cannot fund capital without consuming cash.
findings.figures: £7.025m of capital funded by internal borrowing; CFR at year-end £237.3m
findings.quote: during 2025/26 we have temporarily used cash balances to fund the capital schemes, this is referred to as 'internal borrowing'. There will be a need to replace the internal borrowing with long-term PWLB borrowing during the next financial year.

findings.paper_title: 6. DRAFT ANNUAL GOVERNANCE STATEMENT 2025-26
findings.headline: FOI and information governance capacity overwhelmed by volume and complexity of requests
findings.detail: There is 'an increase in both the volume and complexity of FOI requests submitted, with requests becoming more detailed and resource-intensive with limited team members for both Information Governance and the services responding resulting in targets not being achieved.' This was identified as a governance challenge requiring improvement during the year.
findings.matters: Failure to meet statutory information request deadlines creates regulatory risk and suggests resource constraints; the trend is described as ongoing, not resolved.
findings.figures: No specific request volumes or response times provided
findings.quote: An increase in both the volume and complexity of FOI requests submitted, with requests becoming more detailed and resource-intensive with limited team members for both Information Governance and the services responding resulting in targets not being achieved.

findings.paper_title: 6. DRAFT ANNUAL GOVERNANCE STATEMENT 2025-26
findings.headline: Outstanding objection to 2024-25 accounts relating to The Shay Stadium disposal, not yet concluded by auditors
findings.detail: An elector has objected to the 2024-25 financial statements in relation to the disposal of The Shay Stadium. The external auditors 'have yet to conclude due to the sale not yet being finalised.' This creates uncertainty over whether an audit qualification or adverse finding will be issued on the finalised accounts.
findings.matters: An outstanding audit objection on a major asset disposal is a pending risk to accounts sign-off; disposal proceeds and accounting treatment remain unresolved.
findings.figures: The Shay Stadium (asset name and disposal ongoing)
findings.quote: The Auditors received an objection to the 2024/25 financial statements from an elector. This relates to the disposal of The Shay Stadium, and the Auditors have yet to conclude due to the sale not yet being finalised.

findings.paper_title: 6. DRAFT ANNUAL GOVERNANCE STATEMENT 2025-26
findings.headline: Major new joint venture delivery model launching August 2026 with governance complexity
findings.detail: From August 2026, Calderdale will 'enter a new joint venture delivery model, marking a significant shift in how services are commissioned and delivered.' This transition will 'require enhanced commercial governance, including performance monitoring, risk assessment, and contract management.' The council is working to ensure 'scrutiny arrangements are in place to provide transparency and accountability, and that the joint venture aligns with strategic priorities and public value.'
findings.matters: Major operational transitions create governance risk and require sustained management attention; the statement's language suggests this work is still being finalised (scrutiny arrangements 'to be' in place rather than confirmed).
findings.figures: Launch date: August 2026
findings.quote: From August 2026, Calderdale will enter a new joint venture delivery model, marking a significant shift in how services are commissioned and delivered. This transition will require enhanced commercial governance, including performance monitoring, risk assessment, and contract management.

findings.paper_title: 6. DRAFT ANNUAL GOVERNANCE STATEMENT 2025-26
findings.headline: Emerging trend of increased judicial review challenges to council decisions
findings.detail: The statement identifies 'an emerging trend of increased judicial review challenges, indicating greater legal scrutiny of governance, process integrity, and decision-making quality.' This is flagged as 'the most significant risk identified through this assessment.' There is also 'an increase in stakeholder interest, challenge and concerns raised through various routes including Freedom of Information and Subject Access Requests; Fraud and Whistleblowing concerns and judicial review (public law) challenges,' creating 'a risk to diversion of capacity and resources in responding, costs and settlements.'
findings.matters: Increasing legal challenge to council decisions signals governance or decision-making weaknesses; defending judicial review cases diverts capacity and incurs unbudgeted legal costs and potential settlement costs.
findings.figures: No quantified cost impact provided; risk described as 'emerging trend'
findings.quote: The most significant risk identified through this assessment relates to an emerging trend of increased judicial review challenges, indicating greater legal scrutiny of governance, process integrity, and decision-making quality.

findings.paper_title: 6. DRAFT ANNUAL GOVERNANCE STATEMENT 2025-26
findings.headline: Adult social care costs continuing to grow and driving budget pressures despite improvement efforts
findings.detail: Although improvements were made in some service areas during 2025-26, 'the increasing level of need and cost of adult social care continued to grow.' Forward-looking risk assessment acknowledges the council 'will need to accommodate increasing costs in adult social care' in medium-term financial planning.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled demand growth in adult social care is a known risk factor across local government; this council's inability to arrest the trend despite focused effort signals structural financial vulnerability.
findings.figures: No specific cost or volume figures provided in statement
findings.quote: the increasing level of need and cost of adult social care continued to grow

findings.paper_title: 6. DRAFT ANNUAL GOVERNANCE STATEMENT 2025-26
findings.headline: External auditor's report for 2024-25 identified significant weakness in financial reporting as continuing from prior year
findings.detail: The auditor's Value for Money Arrangements report concluded that a significant weakness in financial reporting arrangements reported in 2023-24 'remains.' Although improvements have been made in timeliness and processes, the council continues to work toward meeting the 30 June deadline for publication of unaudited accounts.
findings.matters: Persistent audit findings on financial reporting undermine confidence in the council's ability to deliver timely, accurate accounts and may signal underlying capacity or process issues in finance function.
findings.figures: Target publication date for 2025-26 unaudited accounts: 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Financial Reporting arrangements – External Auditors annual report 2024/25 concluded the significant weakness reported in 2023/24 remains.

findings.paper_title: 6. DRAFT ANNUAL GOVERNANCE STATEMENT 2025-26
findings.headline: Growing high needs deficit in Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) with long-term sustainability uncertain
findings.detail: Calderdale continues to experience 'a growing high needs deficit within the Dedicated Schools Grant.' While the government will fund 90% of the historic deficit to March 2026 via grant, future funding for 2026-27 onwards 'is still not certain.' The council must submit a SEND Reform Plan to the Department for Education, and the statutory accounting override ends in 2027-28, at which point the deficit must be reflected in general fund accounts.
findings.matters: A materially growing SEND deficit that will hit general fund balances from 2028 onwards is a forward financial risk that must be managed within the Medium-Term Financial Plan; its trajectory is unknown.
findings.figures: 90% of historic deficit to 31 March 2026 funded by government grant; 'statutory accounting override' to end 2027/28
findings.quote: Calderdale, like many councils, continues to experience a growing high needs deficit within the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG). While the statutory override remains in place, the long-term sustainability of SEND funding and the implications for the general fund require close monitoring.

findings.paper_title: 6. DRAFT ANNUAL GOVERNANCE STATEMENT 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal audit concluded governance is 'partially effective' and 'operating but under pressure' with 'particular fragility in high-demand and financially sensitive areas'
findings.detail: The council's Chief Audit Executive delivered an explicitly limited assurance opinion, stating that 'control design and operational effectiveness remain inconsistent' and that 'material improvement is required in several high-risk, high-demand and high-spend areas.' The auditor identified this as requiring 'full rebuild and evidence assurance across all key risk areas.'
findings.matters: Inconsistent control design and gaps in financial management assurance in high-spend areas (adult social care, children's services) mean the council cannot yet provide reliable governance confirmation to external stakeholders, including lenders.
findings.figures: 6 areas identified for improvement priority during 2026-27
findings.quote: Calderdale Metropolitan Borough Council has a partially effective system of governance, risk management and internal control that is operating but under pressure, with particular fragility in high-demand and financially sensitive areas

findings.paper_title: 6. DRAFT ANNUAL GOVERNANCE STATEMENT 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's financial outturn for 2025-26 was an overspend requiring use of risk reserves
findings.detail: The council exceeded its approved budget for the year and had to finance the deficit from its risk reserves. This follows a continuing 'significant weakness' identified by external auditors in the previous year's financial sustainability assessment. The overspend occurred despite improvements in some service areas.
findings.matters: An unbudgeted overspend depleting reserves indicates either planning failures or uncontrolled demand growth; either signals risk to the council's financial trajectory.
findings.figures: 2025-26 overspend, financed from risk reserves (specific amount not quantified in statement)
findings.quote: The financial outturn for 2025/26 presents an overspend against approved budget, creating the need to finance this from risk reserves.

findings.paper_title: item 8 - Final Accounts 2025-26 - Revenue and Capital Outturn Position
findings.headline: Capital programme underspend of £9.77m (13% of budget) may indicate delivery constraints
findings.detail: The council delivered £63.237m of capital expenditure against a £73.007m budget (87% spend rate). The paper notes this is 'broadly in line with previous year's figures,' suggesting normal slippage. However, £9.77m underspend is material.
findings.matters: Persistent capital underspend could indicate challenges in programme delivery or reduced capacity. It pushes costs into future years and may signal delivery risk.
findings.figures: £63.237m actual vs £73.007m budget; £9.77m underspend; 87% spend rate; borrowing £7.025m vs £11.649m budgeted
findings.quote: Total capital expenditure of £63.237m represents 87% of the approved budget of £73.007m reported to Cabinet on 9 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: item 8 - Final Accounts 2025-26 - Revenue and Capital Outturn Position
findings.headline: General fund reserves are only £7.254m and the finance director is flagging reserve depletion as a structural risk
findings.detail: General fund balance sits at £7.254m after using £7.9m to cover the year's overspend. Useable reserves fell from £54.280m to £42.325m. The director explicitly warns the reserve level 'presents a risk' and the council 'should avoid any further depletion.' The replenishment plan is modest (£0.68m in 2026/27).
findings.matters: A general fund of £7.254m provides minimal shock absorption (2.9% of budget). If the council faces another £7-8m overspend, reserves will be exhausted. The finance director's explicit risk warning is a clear flag for lenders about limited financial resilience.
findings.figures: General fund balance £7.254m (2.9% of budget); total useable reserves £42.325m (down from £54.280m)
findings.quote: The level of reserves carried forward into 2026/27 presents a risk and as a consequence the Council should avoid any further depletion.

findings.paper_title: item 8 - Final Accounts 2025-26 - Revenue and Capital Outturn Position
findings.headline: SEND DSG deficit has grown to -£40.634m, up £21.196m in a single year, with recovery mechanism still being refined
findings.detail: The council's accumulated SEND deficit—unfunded high-needs education costs—has nearly doubled to -£40.634m. While central government is introducing a 90% recovery mechanism, the arrangements are still being finalised and conditions around verification are unclear. This sits on the council's balance sheet as a contingent liability.
findings.matters: A -£40.6m contingent liability represents an accumulated deficit in a statutory service. Until recovery is confirmed and paid, this is a real exposure. Further growth in high-needs demand would worsen it.
findings.figures: SEND DSG deficit -£40.634m; prior year -£19.437m; movement -£21.196m in one year
findings.quote: The current position will result in the Council being able to recover 90% of the historical net DSG deficit though the approach to verification of costs, conditions around receipt of funds is still being refined.

findings.paper_title: item 8 - Final Accounts 2025-26 - Revenue and Capital Outturn Position
findings.headline: Adult Services overspent by £6.856m, driven by social care placement costs rising faster than funding
findings.detail: The Adults directorate ran £6.856m over budget (7.3% overspend). Personalised Long Term Support overspent by £4.629m and All Age Disability/Mental Health by £2.958m. The council attributes this to volume and complexity-driven cost increases in the private sector care market—structural cost drivers.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the council's largest budget area and primary driver of the overspend. Unit costs are rising due to complexity of need and private sector market dynamics—structural, not one-off, cost pressures likely to persist.
findings.figures: Adults directorate £6.856m overspend; Personalised Long Term Support £4.629m overspend; All Age Disability £2.958m overspend; Adult budget £94.050m
findings.quote: This includes social care placement costs in Children's and Adult Services. In addition, the unit costs continue to rise due to a combination of more complex levels of need and the way in which the private sector market operates.

findings.paper_title: item 8 - Final Accounts 2025-26 - Revenue and Capital Outturn Position
findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £7.919m (3.17% of budget) being funded by reserves, not from operational surplus
findings.detail: The council spent £257.7m against an approved budget of £249.8m. This £7.9m structural deficit required use of unallocated reserves to balance the books. The position deteriorated progressively through the year before final controls took effect in Q4.
findings.matters: A council running a £7.9m structural deficit—about 3% of budget—is not self-balancing. Funding the gap from reserves is not sustainable and signals that approved budgets are not matching the true cost of delivering services.
findings.figures: £7.919m overspend; £249.8m approved budget; £257.7m actual spend; 3.17% overspend
findings.quote: The Net cost of services for the year was £257.7m which resulted in a net overspend of £7.9m or 3.1% of the approved budget... The final outturn position requires the use of £7.9m from unallocated reserves to present a balanced position at year end.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Demand-led services — Children's and Adult's — overspent by amounts the council could not control within budget
findings.detail: The 2024/25 overspend principally reflects demand and cost pressures in Children's and Adult's services beyond those factored into the budget. The council introduced spending controls but these were insufficient to contain the overspend, indicating these service areas face structural cost growth.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled demand-led service costs (typically statutory obligations) represent a material risk to financial sustainability. If the council cannot manage these services within budget, this is a structural, not cyclical, problem.
findings.figures: £9.2m total overspend driven principally by demand-led services
findings.quote: The Council's overspend in 2024/25 primarily relates to demand-led services including Children's and Adult's services which have experienced additional cost and demand pressures outside of those factored into the 2024/25 budget. The Council had introduced measures to reduce spending pressures on these demand-led services, however these were not sufficient to control the overspend.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Head of Internal Audit issued 'limitation of scope' opinion — insufficient resources to deliver audit plan
findings.detail: The council's Head of Internal Audit reported throughout 2024/25 that audit resources were insufficient to deliver the annual audit plan, and issued a 'limitation of scope' overall opinion at year-end. Auditors identify this as a significant weakness in governance arrangements. The council cannot now gain assurance on the effectiveness of its control environment.
findings.matters: Internal audit is the council's primary mechanism for assuring the board that controls are working. A limitation of scope opinion combined with a disclaimed external audit opinion means the council has no independent assurance over the control environment and governance arrangements.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Through 2024/25 the Council's Head of Internal Audit reported to the Audit Committee the risks to delivering the Audit Plan with the available audit resources. At the end of the year the results of Internal Audit's work and the other sources of assurance, were not sufficient to support a Head of Internal Audit Opinion.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Medium-term funding gaps of £2.9m–£6.1m per year requiring savings delivery that has not been achieved
findings.detail: The MTFP presented in January 2025 identifies base funding gaps of £2.9m for 2025/26, £4.2m for 2026/27, and £6.1m for 2027/28, which must be delivered through cost savings. Given that the council has not controlled spending to meet this year's budget, delivery of three consecutive years of savings is a material execution risk.
findings.matters: Structural funding shortfalls mean the council faces sustained pressure to cut costs or further deplete reserves. A proven inability to hit savings targets increases the likelihood of accelerated reserve drawdown.
findings.quote: The Medium Financial Plan Update presented in January 2025 identified a base funding gap of £2.9m for 2025/26, £4.2m for 2026/27 and £6.1m for 2027/28 which will need to be delivered through cost savings through developing plans to generate savings and efficiencies.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit projected to reach £39m by end of 2025/26 — more than doubling
findings.detail: The DSG deficit for 2024/25 alone was £13.3m. The cumulative deficit stands at £19.4m at year-end 2024/25 and is projected to reach £39m by end of 2025/26 without mitigating actions. Auditors acknowledged this as a risk of significant weakness though concluded current arrangements do not yet reflect this for 2024/25.
findings.matters: Growing education deficits indicate structural cost pressures in schools services that the council cannot absorb. These deficits may eventually cascade into general fund pressures through changes to statutory override or funding arrangements.
findings.figures: £13.3m deficit 2024/25, £19.4m cumulative, £39m projected 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council reported a deficit on its Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) for 2024/25 of £13.3m. The cumulative deficit on the DSG at the end of 2024/25 is £19.4m, and the Council projects the deficit will be £39m by the end of 2025/26 without mitigating actions.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Council is depleting reserves unsustainably to cover recurring overspends — a pattern continuing for two years
findings.detail: 2024/25 overspend was £9.2m (down from projected £12m), funded by £12.3m from reserves. For 2023/24, overspend was £5.7m covered by £11m reserves. The council is now projecting a £2.7m overspend in 2025/26 with £4.6m more reserves to be used. Auditors explicitly identify this as a continuing significant weakness in financial sustainability that remains unresolved.
findings.matters: Sustained reserve drawdown to cover operational deficits indicates the council's revenue budget is structurally unbalanced and cannot sustain service delivery without asset erosion. This threatens the council's financial flexibility and ability to manage future shocks.
findings.figures: 2024/25 overspend £9.2m, reserves used £12.3m; 2023/24 overspend £5.7m, reserves used £11m; 2025/26 projected overspend £2.7m, reserves projected £4.6m
findings.quote: The Council used £12.3m reserves to fund the spending in 2024/25... This will further deplete the Council's reserves available to support earmarked purposes and is unsustainable.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Auditors will disclaim their opinion on the financial statements — no assurance will be provided
findings.detail: Due to government-introduced backstop legislation requiring publication by 27 February 2026, auditors cannot complete sufficient procedures to provide a normal audit opinion. They will instead issue a disclaimed opinion, meaning no opinion is expressed on the financial statements and no assurance is provided. This follows disclaimed opinions from prior years, leaving gaps in assurance over opening balances.
findings.matters: Lenders typically rely on audited financial statements as a core assurance mechanism. A disclaimer means the council's accounts carry no third-party validation and predecessor auditor disclaimed opinions create multiple years of unassured positions.
findings.figures: Backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: It has not been possible to complete sufficient procedures as part of the current year's audit to enable us to issue a non-disclaimed opinion. For this reason, we will be issuing a disclaimed opinion in time for the Council to publish its financial statements by the backstop date of 27 February 2026 as required by the relevant legislation.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement
findings.headline: The council is depleting cash reserves to avoid locking into long-term borrowing at 5.87%, reducing financial flexibility
findings.detail: Under-borrowing—using cash balances instead of taking long-term debt—stands at £78.8m in 2025/26 and is expected to shrink to £20.9m by 2028/29. The strategy is deliberate rate-timing: waiting for base rate cuts before committing to 25-year PWLB rates currently averaging 5.87%. This preserves optionality but depletes the buffer available for unexpected shocks.
findings.matters: While rate timing is rational, drawing down reserves to fund operations and capital reduces the council's ability to absorb revenue shortfalls or unexpected costs—a key credit concern.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing £78.8m (2025/26) declining to £20.9m (2028/29). PWLB 24.5-25 year rate 5.87% average in 2025/26. Base rate 3.75%, down from 4.50%.
findings.quote: we are maximising internal borrowing (use of cash balances) and minimising long term borrowing where possible (as liquidity requirements allow) until at least 2026/27 when the forecast is that the base rate might be reduced

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement
findings.headline: Financing costs are rising from 4.2% to 8.2% of net revenue by 2028/29, signalling tightening budget headroom
findings.detail: The proportion of revenue devoted to debt service (interest, MRP and investment income) is climbing sharply over three years. The council attributes this explicitly to both higher MRP charges from the expanded capital programme and rising interest costs. At 8.2% of net revenue, this is material constraint on service flexibility.
findings.matters: Rising debt service is inelastic—it must be paid before services. A rapid increase signals the council is approaching the limits of what its revenue base can support, with implications for financial resilience.
findings.quote: What this indicator highlights is that the ratio is increasing from 2025/26 (mainly due to higher Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charges as a result of a larger capital programme and rising borrowing costs due to interest rates going up).

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement
findings.headline: Capital spending is doubling to £137.4m in 2026/27, driving the Capital Financing Requirement up to £319.5m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's capital expenditure forecast jumps from £73.0m in 2025/26 to £137.4m in 2026/27—nearly 90% growth. This is driven by West Yorkshire Combined Authority funded schemes (Transport and Transforming Cities Fund) moving to delivery stage. The underlying borrowing need (CFR) rises from £246.7m to £319.5m over the three-year period, a net addition of £72.8m.
findings.matters: A major step-change in capital commitments locks the council into higher debt service costs for decades; a lender needs to understand what assets are being funded and whether revenue can sustain the debt.
findings.quote: Capital expenditure is forecast to be higher in future years, in part because several capital schemes in relation to the Council's West Yorkshire + Transport and Transforming Cities Fund have progressed through the West Yorkshire Combined Authority Assurance Framework to the delivery stage.

findings.paper_title: Item 7c - Cabinet Budget Proposals - Re2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Capital program of £451.3m over 4 years includes £167.4m of borrowing costs and schemes in areas of known challenge (SEND, highways, leisure).
findings.detail: The revised capital programme totals £451.3m across 2025/26–2028/29, funded by £261.2m external grants and borrowing. Borrowing-funded schemes include schools improvement, vehicle/refuse fleet replacement, Clifton Business Park regeneration, children's residential homes, Halifax Leisure Centre, and £4m annual highways maintenance. Revenue costs of borrowing are estimated at £167.4m over the programme life. While the council notes it has "low levels of borrowing" currently, this represents a material new commitment on the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Capital borrowing locks in revenue costs across multiple budget years. Given the council's tight medium-term position and rising social care pressures, this borrowing must be justified by returns that offset costs. Leisure and regeneration schemes carry delivery and demand risk.
findings.figures: Capital programme 2025/26–2028/29: £451.3m; External grant funding: £261.2m; Borrowing revenue costs: £167.4m; Highways maintenance allocation: £4m pa; New SEND school and places: 200+ additional places
findings.quote: The proposed budget incorporates the revenue costs associated with borrowing (£167.4m over the life of the programme). Schemes in the revised capital programme funded from Borrowing, include: Schools Improvement and Maintenance, Vehicle Replacement, including Refuse Fleet, Garden Communities and Clifton Business Park, Children's Residential Provision, Halifax Leisure Centre, New allocation of £4m pa for Highways Maintenance, Children's Playground replacement

findings.paper_title: Item 7c - Cabinet Budget Proposals - Re2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Council Tax increasing to 4.99% maximum with 74–84% of new funding coming from local taxation rather than central government.
findings.detail: The budget includes a 2.99% general council tax increase plus a 2% Adult Social Care precept, totalling 4.99%—the maximum allowable without referendum. Notably, central government funding reforms mean the share of new funding from Council Tax is rising: 74% in 2026/27 and 84% in 2027/28–2028/29. This represents growing structural dependence on local taxation, which is capped by referendum limits and household ability to pay.
findings.matters: A council relying on maximum council tax increases to balance its budget faces risk if: (a) taxpayers resist further increases; (b) the tax base shrinks; or (c) government reduces grant faster than forecast. The shift from grant to council tax income removes central government risk-sharing.
findings.figures: Council tax increase 2026/27: 4.99%; Share of new CSP from council tax: 74% (2026/27), 84% (2027–2028/29)
findings.quote: The share of new funding that comes from Council Tax is higher than recent years at 74% in 2026/27 and 84% in the final 2-years of the settlement.

findings.paper_title: Item 7c - Cabinet Budget Proposals - Re2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Service pressures totalling £21.4m forecast for 2026/27, concentrated in social care and transport.
findings.detail: In-year and demand pressures identified total £10.974m and £10.412m respectively. The largest single pressure is Adults Social Care at £9.068m (in-year £3.753m, demand £5.315m). Children's Social Care and SEND shows £2.149m (in-year £1.426m, demand £0.723m). Highways Maintenance is £2.2m and Home to School Transport £1m. These pressures are meeting the council's attempt at savings of only £5.24m, leaving a net increase in cost base.
findings.matters: The council is experiencing structural cost pressures in services (particularly social care) that savings programs are only partially offsetting. This suggests the council is managing demand growth rather than controlling underlying costs, which limits future flexibility.
findings.figures: Total pressures: £21.386m (in-year £10.974m + demand £10.412m); Adults Social Care: £9.068m; Children's/SEND: £2.149m; Highways: £2.2m; Home to School Transport: £1m
findings.quote: The areas with the most significant cost pressures are adult's and children's social care, special educational needs, highways and waste management.

findings.paper_title: Item 7c - Cabinet Budget Proposals - Re2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Council acknowledges that its reserves are inadequate to cover identified risks even with planned growth.
findings.detail: The council's General Fund Balance Reserve is £7.254m at 1 April 2025 and will grow to £12.2m by 31 March 2029. However, the Chief Finance Officer's section 25 statement confirms that "the level of reserves is unlikely to provide the financial cover should all the identified risks materialise." Total corporate and earmarked reserves on 31 March 2026 are estimated at £29.53m in base case or £24m in a worst-case scenario. The council plans to contribute £0.68m, £1.68m, and £2.68m to reserves in successive years.
findings.matters: Inadequate reserves limit the council's ability to absorb budget shocks, manage in-year pressures, or bridge unexpected gaps. Combined with growing pressures in social care and SEND, this signals constrained financial flexibility.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance: £7.254m (1 April 2025) → £12.2m (31 March 2029); Total reserves (worst case): £24m; Planned contributions: £0.68m (2026/27), £1.68m (2027/28), £2.68m (2028/29)
findings.quote: It is currently estimated that the balance of these categories of reserves on 31 March 2026 will be £29.53. For the purposes of this budget report the worst-case scenario, taking account of the in-year outturn forecast report to Cabinet in November 2025 would reduce the balance available to c£24m. The level of reserves is unlikely to provide the financial cover should all the identified risks materialise.

findings.paper_title: Item 7c - Cabinet Budget Proposals - Re2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: No comprehensive savings plan yet in place for a cumulative budget gap of £6.8m in 2027/28–2028/29.
findings.detail: While the 2026/27 budget is balanced, the council forecasts a cumulative in-year deficit of £3.7m in 2027/28 and £6.8m by 2028/29. The budget report explicitly states that formulating a "robust and achievable savings plan" is deferred to Q1 2026/27, to be developed in conjunction with the Finance Improvement Plan. No detail is provided on what savings options are under consideration or how realistic they are.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council has credible plans to address forecast deficits. A deferred savings plan for 18+ months ahead—without documented options—raises questions about whether the council's financial outlook is genuinely sustainable or dependent on unproven options.
findings.figures: 2027/28 projected gap: £3.7m; 2028/29 cumulative gap: £6.8m
findings.quote: To achieve this level of savings in a meaningful way requires a comprehensive plan based upon a range of option appraisals. This is a priority for the first quarter of the new year and will be developed in conjunction with the Finance Improvement Plan.

findings.paper_title: Item 8 - Capital Investment Strategy 2026-27 and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Highway maintenance demand continues to exceed available budget despite investment, with the deteriorating network creating an ongoing structural pressure.
findings.detail: The council has a legal duty to maintain the adopted highway network (1,100km of roads, 730km walls, 207 bridges). Annual condition surveys show the network continues to deteriorate, resulting in demand for planned and reactive maintenance that 'in recent years has exceeded the available capital and revenue maintenance budgets'. The council is adding £4m per annum (£12m total) over the next three years.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about a statutory obligation (highway maintenance) where demand consistently exceeds available funding, suggesting ongoing budget pressure and potential future claims on council resources.
findings.figures: £4m per annum additional funding for 3 years (£12m total); network comprises 1,100km roads, 730km walls, 207 bridges, 30,500 streetlights
findings.quote: Our annual condition surveys show that the network continues to deteriorate, resulting in an increase in demand for planned and reactive maintenance that in recent years has exceeded the available capital and revenue maintenance budgets.

findings.paper_title: Item 8 - Capital Investment Strategy 2026-27 and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Halifax Leisure Centre requires an additional £4.487m after earlier pause and major affordability review, indicating project delivery and cost control risks.
findings.detail: The leisure centre project was paused in January 2023 after reaching RIBA Stage 4 design due to contractor changes, extreme inflationary increases, and a volatile construction market. A two-phase feasibility review was undertaken. Despite market-testing and independent validation by quantity surveyors, a further £4.487m is now required to complete the scheme, bringing total forecast to £36.4m.
findings.matters: A lender would flag this as evidence of project delivery challenges and cost inflation that could signal broader risks in the council's ability to control capital scheme costs and complete projects within budget.
findings.figures: £4.487m additional funding required; total project cost £36.357m; original pause January 2023; Phase 1 review June 2023
findings.quote: owing to a significant number of external challenges, including contractor changes, extreme inflationary increases and a volatile and saturated construction market, it became clear that project costs were likely to escalate beyond the approved budget... it is forecast that an additional £4.487m in funding will be required to complete the scheme

findings.paper_title: Item 8 - Capital Investment Strategy 2026-27 and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Capital financing costs growing to £26.0m annually by 2028/29, reaching 8% of net revenue stream and approaching the CFO's 10% prudent limit.
findings.detail: Borrowing requirements of £167.4m across the programme will generate annual revenue costs of £15.1m (2026/27), £21.3m (2027/28), and £26.0m (2028/29). The Director of Resources & Transformation has set a prudent limit that capital financing costs should not exceed 10% of net revenue stream. By 2028/29, the council is projected to reach 8%, leaving only 2% headroom before hitting the stated prudent limit.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about diminishing financial flexibility as debt service costs grow and approach the prudent limit, potentially constraining future borrowing capacity or forcing difficult choices between capital investment and service delivery.
findings.figures: £15.1m (2026/27), £21.3m (2027/28), £26.0m (2028/29); CFO prudent limit 10%; current level by 2028/29 reaches 8%
findings.quote: The total cost of borrowing include in the Revenue Budget is £15.1m, £21.3m and £26.0m for 2026/27, 2027/28 and 2028/29 respectively... The Chief Financial Officer has determined that the prudent limit for the Council's capital financing costs as a proportion of the net revenue stream should not exceed 10%. The current level by 2028/29 reaches 8%.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Dedicated Schools Grant - High Needs Block Deficit Update
findings.headline: Sharp growth in SEND assessments, particularly Autism (214% increase in four years)
findings.detail: Children with EHCPs for Autism have grown from 394 (2022/23) to 674 (2024/25). This increase is driving placement demand that exceeds the capacity of the three maintained specialist schools and forces reliance on expensive independent provision.
findings.matters: Rapid growth in statutory service demand that outpaces both capacity and funding signals structural service pressure with no easy resolution, particularly given that placement decisions are partly driven by parental legal rights.
findings.figures: Autism EHCPs: 394 (2022/23) to 674 (2024/25); total EHCPs now 2,900 (Nov 2025); all three maintained specialist schools are full
findings.quote: In Calderdale over the last 3 years there has been a sharp increase in children being assessed as requiring an Education Health and Care Plan (EHCP).

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Dedicated Schools Grant - High Needs Block Deficit Update
findings.headline: Ending of Statutory Override presents financial risk unless deficit is controlled
findings.detail: The council is taking actions to ensure that when the Statutory Override ends, the accumulated DSG deficit does not threaten the overall council budget. This indicates concern about what happens when the override expires and deficits must be managed within the general fund.
findings.matters: The Statutory Override has allowed councils to accumulate DSG deficits outside the general fund. When it ends, unresolved deficits will impact the council's overall financial position and may constrain borrowing or service spending.
findings.figures: £39m cumulative deficit by April 2026
findings.quote: actions are being taken to mitigate the increased pressures and ensure the ending of the Statutory Override does not present an existential threat to the Council's budget

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Dedicated Schools Grant - High Needs Block Deficit Update
findings.headline: DSG deficit not expected to balance before 2028, creating multi-year structural problem
findings.detail: Despite multiple mitigation actions (establishment of new specialist schools, expanding mainstream provision, improved decision-making processes), the council does not forecast the High Needs Block to reach balance by 2028. A one-year report review is planned, suggesting ongoing uncertainty.
findings.matters: A multi-year unresolved deficit in a statutory service indicates the council faces persistent budget pressure that will require either significant service reconfiguration or drawing on reserves or other budgets.
findings.figures: Unmitigated deficit trajectory calculated; even mitigated position shows continued pressure to 2028
findings.quote: Even with mitigations, it is not anticipated that the DSG High Needs Block will balance by 2028

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Dedicated Schools Grant - High Needs Block Deficit Update
findings.headline: Government funding has not kept pace with rising demand and costs for SEND provision
findings.detail: Independent Specialist Provision costs have risen sharply (from £49k to £74k per placement) and the number of children requiring these placements has nearly doubled in two years, but government HNB grants have not increased at the same rate, creating a structural funding gap.
findings.matters: When a council's statutory obligations grow faster than government funding, the deficit becomes structural rather than cyclical, signalling a long-term financial pressure unlikely to resolve without intervention or service change.
findings.figures: ISP average costs rose from £49k (2023) to £74k (current); ISP placements increased from 121 to 217 between March 2023 and March 2025
findings.quote: Over recent years there has also been a very large increase in costs of provision and Government HNB grants have not kept in line with the demand and cost increases experienced.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Dedicated Schools Grant - High Needs Block Deficit Update
findings.headline: Cumulative High Needs deficit forecast at over £39m by April 2026, with £19m in-year overspend
findings.detail: The deficit stems from a sharp rise in children assessed as needing Education Health and Care Plans and placement in expensive Independent Specialist Provision. The in-year overspend has escalated from £6m (2023/24) to £19m (2025/26). The council has a statutory duty to fund these placements.
findings.matters: A council with a structural, growing deficit in a non-discretionary statutory service signals difficulty managing its budget pressures and raises questions about financial resilience.
findings.figures: £39m cumulative deficit forecast by April 2026; £19m in-year overspend 2025/26; ISP numbers rose from 121 (March 2023, cost £6m) to 217 (March 2025, cost £14m); average ISP placement cost risen from £49k to £74k
findings.quote: the current in-year overspend being forecast at £19m by the end of the current financial year, with a cumulative High Needs deficit of over £39m forecast by April 2026

news_drafts.headline: Investment interest income fell £1.54m short of budget (£966k actual vs £2.12m budgeted)
news_drafts.lead: This shortfall is a direct consequence of reserve drawdown to cover service deficits, and it reduces the income available to offset borrowing costs and treasury management expenses.
news_drafts.paper_title: 8. Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 Audit Committee 27 July 2026 v2

news_drafts.headline: Treasury management costs exceeded budget by £654k (6.4% overspend)
news_drafts.lead: Treasury costs are largely fixed and crowding-out for service spending. A budget miss here indicates broader cash pressures are forcing higher-than-expected borrowing or refinancing costs.
news_drafts.paper_title: 8. Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 Audit Committee 27 July 2026 v2

news_drafts.headline: Council is using short-term borrowing (25 bps cheaper than PWLB) betting on rate cuts by December 2027 for refinancing
news_drafts.lead: If rates do not fall as forecast, or fall too slowly, the council faces refinancing risk at higher rates than currently assumed, adding to treasury costs. This is an active rate-bet rather than passive debt management.
